worksheet.title: Loop a Longer Pattern
worksheet.subtitle: Ontario Math C3.1 — repeating events
worksheet.learning_goal: I can loop a pattern that has more than one action inside.

parts.title: A pattern with more parts
text: A drum beat can be clap, clap, stomp — clap, clap, stomp. The whole group repeats.
A loop runs EVERY block inside it each time around. So a loop with three actions repeats all three together. Count how many of each Bit does.

parts.title: Read this loop
parts.note: Three actions inside (clap, clap, stomp) all run each repeat. 4 repeats = 12 actions in all.

parts.caption: The 3-action group is one repeat — the loop does it 4 times.

parts.title: Count it
parts.prompt: The loop is repeat 4 with clap, clap, stomp inside. How many actions in ONE repeat? ______  How many actions in TOTAL? ______

parts.title: Predict, then check
parts.prompt: Change repeat 4 to repeat 5. PREDICT: how many STOMPS does Bit do? How many CLAPS? Then check.

parts.title: Write your own
parts.prompt: Bit's pattern is wave, wave, bow. To do the whole pattern 4 times, fill in: repeat ______. How many WAVES is that in total? ______

parts.title: Challenge
parts.prompt: Bit's loop did 6 STOMPS. The pattern inside has 1 stomp each repeat. How many times did the loop repeat? How do you know?

parts.title: Big idea
parts.text: When a loop has more than one block inside, ALL of them run each repeat. To count one action, multiply how many per repeat by the number of repeats.

parts.title: What this worksheet teaches
parts.text: A loop runs every block inside it each time, so a multi-action pattern repeats as a unit. Students count each action across the repeats by multiplying, and work backwards from a total. No coding experience needed.

parts.title: Before you start
parts.text: No computer needed — the worksheet shows the blocks and what Bit does, so you can teach from the printout. Optional: a Scratch-style app to drag the blocks and watch Bit run — you only press the green flag.

parts.title: How to lead it (about 30 minutes)
text: 1. Show it (you do). The pattern clap, clap, stomp is 3 actions; 4 repeats make 12 actions.
2. Do one together. Exercise 1 — 3 actions per repeat, 12 in total.
3. Let them work. Students count each action type (Ex 2), write a repeat (Ex 3), and work backwards from a total (Ex 4).

parts.title: Answer key (these are the verified correct answers)
text: Exercise 1 — 3 actions per repeat; 12 actions total. Exercise 2 — 5 stomps and 10 claps.
Exercise 3 — repeat 4; 8 waves total. Exercise 4 (challenge) — 6 repeats (6 stomps ÷ 1 stomp per repeat).

parts.title: If students get stuck — and ways to adjust
text: Watch for: counting the whole pattern as one action. Count each kind of action separately.
Make it easier: count how many of one action are in a single repeat, then multiply.
Make it harder: ask the total claps for the pattern repeated 7 times.

parts.title: Ontario curriculum link (official wording)
text: C3.1 — solve problems and create computational representations of mathematical situations by writing and executing code, including code that involves sequential, concurrent, and repeating events.
In plain terms: students write and run step-by-step instructions — including a "repeat" instruction — to make something happen.
C3.2 — read and alter existing code, including code that involves sequential, concurrent, and repeating events, and describe how changes to the code affect the outcomes.
In plain terms: students read instructions, change one, and explain what the change did to the result.

parts.title: You'll know it worked when
parts.text: The child multiplies each action by the repeats and works backwards from a total.
